title: The Girl from Yara: the Mariana Grajales Platoon and Cuba's First Woman General
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Yara: born on the ninth of December
stops.date_confidence: Birth date 9 December 1940 is attested by English Wikipedia and by the 2023 Havana candidate profile. Yara as birthplace is given by Wikipedia and by municipal sources; the National Assembly's own profile page instead gives San Miguel del Padrón, Havana, which is her present electoral district. The contradiction is recorded, not resolved. Coordinate corrected to the town of Yara, Granma, at 20 degrees 16 minutes 36 seconds north, 76 degrees 56 minutes 49 seconds west; the figure carried in the research pool sat about 14 km out in farmland.
stops.campa: On the cane plain below the Sierra Maestra, in what is then Oriente province, a daughter is registered as Delsa Esther Puebla Viltres. The town is Yara, where the Spanish burned the cacique Hatuey four centuries earlier and where the sugar country runs up against the first hills. Her family works land it does not own. The household calls her Teté, a diminutive that will outlast every rank the state gives her. She is the eldest of eight. Two of her brothers go up to the Rebel Army; so, at sixteen, does she.
suggested_refs: Civil registry of Yara, Granma province, for the 1940 birth entry
sources: Asamblea Nacional del Poder Popular, deputy profile, parlamentocubano.gob.cu/delsa-esther-puebla-viltre

stops.name: Yara: the grandparents' house
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction from Puebla's own retrospective testimony in Marianas en combate (Pathfinder Press, 2003), given in interviews of 2000 and 2002. No vital or genealogical record was reached to corroborate the household arrangement or the count of eight children. The date is an ordering device for the childhood years, not an attested event.
stops.campa: She is raised chiefly by her grandparents. Almost everything known about these years comes from a woman in her sixties answering an interviewer's questions in Havana, sixty years and one revolution downstream of them. What the family has instead of money is land worked for somebody else and the ordinary rural arithmetic of the Cuban 1940s: no doctor within reach, no secondary school in the town, a priest who comes when he comes, and one road, which goes to Manzanillo. The house is too poor to buy toys, so her grandmother sews dolls out of cloth.
suggested_refs: Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003, the childhood chapters
sources: Teté Puebla, Marianas in Combat / Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003 (primary text not directly accessible; publisher page and secondary paraphrase only)

stops.name: Manzanillo: the Escuela Normal para Maestros
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The enrolment at fifteen in the first year of the Escuela Normal para Maestros de Manzanillo traces only to Puebla's own oral history; no institutional register or school record was reached, and the month is unknown, so the date defaults to January. The coordinate is the corpus's canonical Manzanillo pin.
stops.campa: At fifteen she enters the first year of the teachers' college at Manzanillo, the port where the sugar of the Cauto valley is shipped out and where the underground is already thick on the ground. The plan is a classroom in some small place like the one she came from. Manzanillo in 1956 is also the town of Celia Sánchez, who is putting together the arms route between the coast and the mountains, and it is not a big town. Puebla completes the first year. She does not enrol for a second.
suggested_refs: Records of the Escuela Normal para Maestros de Manzanillo, mid-1950s
sources: Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003
celia_sanchez.journey.json, Manzanillo stops, for the canonical coordinate

stops.name: Manzanillo: the accusation at the barracks
stops.date_confidence: Uncorroborated. Puebla alleged decades later, in Marianas en combate, that her relative Amelia Puebla and Georgina Barbán were raped by Batista soldiers at the Manzanillo barracks, and gave this as the thing that turned her toward armed struggle. No judicial, medical, or contemporaneous press record was found by either research pass. The date is an ordering device only; the month is not known.
stops.campa: She names, forty years afterward, the thing she says decided her: two women of her own circle, one of them a relative, taken into the army barracks at Manzanillo by Batista's soldiers. There is no file on it, no newspaper notice, no medical record and no complaint. There is a woman in her sixties telling an interviewer in Havana what she was told at fifteen. Within months of hearing it she was carrying dynamite out of Manzanillo for the Movimiento 26 de Julio.
suggested_refs: Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003, on the Manzanillo barracks
sources: Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003 (single source, retrospective, uncorroborated)

stops.name: Manzanillo: sworn into the Movimiento 26 de Julio
stops.date_confidence: Membership of the M-26-7 from age fifteen, in 1956, is attested by English Wikipedia and by her own oral history, cross-checked. The specific month is not attested; September is an ordering choice inside the attested year.
stops.campa: She joins the Movimiento 26 de Julio at fifteen and is given the work the movement hands to people nobody stops and searches: selling bonds, carrying messages, and moving medicine, money, dynamite, rifles and men out of the lowland towns toward the hills. The corridor she works is the one Celia Sánchez is assembling between Manzanillo and the Sierra Maestra. A column of armed men on that road is a battle. A schoolgirl on the same road, carrying a parcel wrapped in brown paper and tied with string, is a schoolgirl.
suggested_refs: M-26-7 bond receipts and courier records for the Manzanillo llano network, 1956-1957
sources: Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003

stops.name: Yara: caltrops on the street
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, single-sourced. The 19 March 1957 caltrop and wire-cutting action at Yara appears only in Puebla's own retrospective memoir. No contemporaneous police report or press notice was located by either research pass, and no second source carries the date. The original pass tagged it attested; the verification pass overturned that as a tagging error.
stops.campa: Whether it happened on the nineteenth of March, or in that month, or at all in the form she later described, rests on one book published in New York in 2003. In that account metal spikes go down on the streets of Yara and the electrical lines come down with them, and for a while the town does not move and does not light. She organises it and takes part in it. She is sixteen. The action costs nobody anything except the tyres and the wires, which is the point of an action run by teenagers with no guns.
suggested_refs: Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003, on the Yara sabotage
sources: Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003 (sole source)

stops.name: Blanquizal: the route given up under torture
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The 12 July 1957 departure from Blanquizal is credited in the research dossier to the Council of State's Diario de la Guerra 3, but neither pass was able to read that passage: the first could not fetch the PDF, the second retrieved unreadable binary. Blanquizal itself could not be located, so the coordinate is the municipal seat of Bartolomé Masó, an approximation flagged as such.
stops.campa: A captured member of the movement gives up the Santiago to Manzanillo arms route under torture, and the network decides she is burned. She goes out of the lowlands on foot with a small group, toward a guerrilla force that has been in the mountains seven months and is not yet certain to last the year. The climb is not a march in formation. People carry each other's loads until they cannot carry them, and the ones who fall behind are collected by the ones who have not yet fallen behind.
stops.quote: Someone would get tired, and another comrade would come by and put his backpack on top of him. There was a time, around 1957, when I was alone up there, until Celia came up.
stops.quote_source: Teté Puebla, quoted in 'Teté, a Woman Who Learned from Fidel,' Periódico 26, 2025, English-language edition
suggested_refs: Heberto Norman Acosta, Diario de la Guerra 3, Oficina de Publicaciones del Consejo de Estado, Havana, 2015
sources: Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003
Periódico 26, 'Teté, a Woman Who Learned from Fidel,' periodico26.cu

stops.name: Sierra Maestra: received into Column One
stops.date_confidence: The arrival is attested; the precise day is contested. Diario de la Guerra 3, page 299, names her among the arrivals and is the ground for 1 August 1957, and the second research pass extracted that page directly with pypdf. EcuRed gives only 'julio de 1957' and quotes her saying 'En julio de 1957 subí a la Sierra Maestra.' Ileana Rodés is named in the diary text; Eugenia Verdecia only in her memoir. The coordinate is a deliberately approximate Sierra Maestra placement: the Comandancia de la Plata did not yet exist in 1957 and she must not be staged there.
stops.campa: She reaches Fidel Castro's column in the mountains at sixteen, one of three girls arriving out of the plain with the army and the police behind them. The force she joins holds no fixed ground and keeps no address; the state it will become is a year of walking away. She is put into Sanidad, the medical service, which in a guerrilla column means carrying what the wounded need up slopes that mules refuse and boiling water for a doctor who is also an infantryman. The war diary of the Council of State enters her by name, age, and town.
stops.quote: Las otras dos muchachas son Delsa Esther Puebla, Teté, de Yara y con solo dieciséis años, e Ileana Rodés, ambas ya con una historia de lucha y buscadas por el ejército y la policía.
stops.quote_source: Heberto Norman Acosta, Diario de la Guerra 3: Del Uvero al primer combate de Pino del Agua, Oficina de Publicaciones del Consejo de Estado, Havana, 2015, p. 299
suggested_refs: Diario de la Guerra 3, p. 299, for the arrival entry
sources: Heberto Norman Acosta, Diario de la Guerra 3 (2015), p. 299, extracted directly from the publisher PDF

stops.name: El Hombrito: the fever
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction from Puebla's oral history, Marianas en combate. The illness, the weeks of recovery at El Hombrito, and Guevara reading poetry to the troops are her account alone; no camp record or second witness was reached. The day is unknown and defaults to the first of the month. Coordinate is the corpus's existing El Hombrito pin.
stops.campa: A fever takes her and does not break for weeks, and she is left to recover at the camp Ernesto Guevara is building at El Hombrito, where there is a bakery, an oven, a printing press and a doctor who is also a commander. He looks in on her. In the evenings he reads poetry aloud to men who mostly cannot read it for themselves. Whether she was on her feet for any of the fighting of that autumn her own account does not say, and whether anyone else was watching closely enough to know, it does not say either. She rejoins the column in December.
suggested_refs: Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003, on El Hombrito
sources: Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003
che_guevara.journey.json, stop 'El Hombrito, the guerrilla republic', for the canonical coordinate

stops.name: Altos de Mompié: the white flag at half past five
stops.date_confidence: The mission is attested and multiply reported; the paperwork is not. Cubainformación's published version of her own detailed telling gives the departure from Altos de Mompié at about 5.30 in the morning, on a mule, with a white flag. Guevara's letter of 22 July 1958 naming 'compañera Teté Puebla, del servicio de Sanidad' is cited in the dossier but neither pass located its text, so that phrase stays unverified at source. The coordinate is an explicitly approximate sierra placement: EcuRed and Granma put Altos de Mompié at about 1,200 metres in the mountains of Bartolomé Masó, well above and south of the town.
stops.campa: More than two hundred captured government soldiers are sitting in rebel hands and the Rebel Army wants them off its books and into the Red Cross. Guevara picks the emissary: a seventeen-year-old out of the medical service, unarmed, because an armed man crossing the lines is a target and a girl on a mule with a white flag is a problem the other side has to think about. She leaves the ridge at about half past five in the morning. Bombing frightens the mule and she goes the rest of the way on foot.
suggested_refs: Ernesto Guevara, letter of 22 July 1958 on the prisoner transfer, cited but not located
sources: Cubainformación, 'Teté Puebla: La Generala, en persona,' interview by Luis Báez

stops.name: Las Vegas de Jibacoa: the armband she will not take off
stops.date_confidence: The destination is attested by Cubainformación's account of her testimony: the enemy camp at Las Vegas de Jibacoa, a consejo popular of Bartolomé Masó municipality in the Yara river valley. That the enemy commander Merob Sosa accepted the truce, and that Castro and Guevara had the answer back by six that evening, come from the same account. The officer she names as 'Captain Durán Batista,' who demanded she remove her armband, appears in no source either pass reached and is memoir-only. Coordinate is approximate to the consejo popular, not landmark-precise.
stops.campa: She reaches the army camp at Las Vegas de Jibacoa about midday. An officer tells her to take the 26 de Julio armband off before she is received. She refuses, and waits in the sun wearing it, until the enemy commander Merob Sosa comes out and hears the terms she was sent with. Sosa accepts the truce. By six that evening the answer is back in the mountains with the men who sent her. She is seventeen. She is carrying no weapon and no rank, and the armband is still on her arm.
suggested_refs: Cubainformación's transcript of Puebla's account of the July 1958 truce mission
sources: Cubainformación, 'Teté Puebla: La Generala, en persona,' interview by Luis Báez
Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003

stops.name: Las Vegas de Jibacoa: two hundred and fifty-seven handed over
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Cubainformación's account gives the handover on 23 July 1958, with International Committee of the Red Cross delegates René Jecquier and Pierre Schoenholzer receiving 257 prisoners, 23 of them wounded. The dossier's earlier vaguer formula, 'more than two hundred,' is superseded by that figure. Puebla's personal presence at the handover itself, as distinct from the previous day's negotiation, is not separately documented.
stops.campa: The next day the delegates of the International Committee of the Red Cross, René Jecquier and Pierre Schoenholzer, take receipt of two hundred and fifty-seven government soldiers, twenty-three of them wounded. The rebels are rid of a burden they cannot feed and gain a photograph of themselves obeying the laws of war. The soldiers go home. Some of them will be captured a second time inside the year, since the war has five months left in it and Oriente is not a large place.
suggested_refs: ICRC delegation records for Cuba, July 1958, naming Jecquier and Schoenholzer
sources: Cubainformación, 'Teté Puebla: La Generala, en persona,' interview by Luis Báez

stops.name: Santiago de Cuba: three trips for medicine
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction from Puebla's oral history alone. Three clandestine journeys to Santiago de Cuba after the truce mission, to restore rebel communications and obtain medical and other supplies, are not corroborated by any independent record reached. The day is an ordering device inside the attested month of the truce mission. Coordinate is the corpus's canonical Santiago de Cuba pin.
stops.campa: After the truce she is sent down out of the mountains three times into Santiago de Cuba, to repair the communications the arrests broke and to buy what the sierra cannot make: antibiotics, surgical thread, batteries, boots. Santiago is the most heavily policed city in the country and the one where the movement has lost the most people. She travels as what she is, a girl of seventeen on a bus, and the papers in her pocket have somebody else's name on them. No independent record of any of the three trips has been found.
suggested_refs: Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003, on the Santiago supply runs
sources: Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003 (sole source)

stops.name: La Comandancia de la Plata: the coin at fifty metres
stops.date_confidence: Date, place and command structure are attested and independently confirmed by Spanish Wikipedia's article on Las Marianas and by Granma's 2014 retrospective on Isabel Rielo. The shooting distance is contradictory: Granma 2014 gives fifty metres with the coin-splitting detail and quotes Puebla directly; the twenty to thirty metres of her Pathfinder oral history could not be confirmed in any source either pass reached, since neither read the book. Both figures are recorded; neither is adjudicated. Coordinate is the corpus's existing La Plata pin.
stops.campa: Castro spends about seven hours arguing down his own commanders, who do not want rifles given to women while men in the column are still carrying sticks. He gives the rifles anyway, thirteen of them, and names the unit for Mariana Grajales, the mother of the Maceos. Then he sets a marksmanship trial to decide who will lead it. Isabel Rielo shoots better that day. Puebla is made second in command and stays second in command for the rest of the war.
stops.quote: Llegó el momento de decidir la jefatura del pelotón (…) la meta era partir una moneda a 50 metros de distancia. Tenía buena puntería, pero ese día Isabel Rielo la tuvo mejor. Quedé como segunda al mando.
stops.quote_source: Teté Puebla, quoted in Granma, 'Dos 9 de abril, una misma visión revolucionaria,' 9 April 2014
suggested_refs: Granma, 'Dos 9 de abril, una misma visión revolucionaria,' 9 April 2014, on Isabel Rielo and the marksmanship trial
sources: fidel_castro.journey.json, stop 'La Comandancia de la Plata: the state under the canopy'

stops.name: La Comandancia de la Plata: the clothes Celia chose
stops.date_confidence: The detail is attested as Puebla's own account, published in Bohemia's feature 'Gardenias guerrilleras.' The date is an ordering device set immediately after the attested platoon formation of 4 September 1958; no source gives a day for the issue of uniforms. Coordinate is the corpus's existing La Plata pin.
stops.campa: Celia Sánchez, who runs the supply lines, the hospitals, the armoury and the couriers of the whole sierra, decides what the thirteen women will wear. Not the men's uniform. Something cut like the one she wears herself, without buttons down the front. Puebla is twenty-two days short of her first battle and is being fitted for it. She names Sánchez, afterward and in every interview she gives across the next sixty years, as the person she learned the work from, and she uses very nearly the same sentence to do it each time.
stops.quote: Celia escogió hasta la ropa a usar, no era igual a la de los hombres, sino como la que ella misma llevaba en esos momentos, sin botones delante porque, eso sí, ¡éramos muy femeninas!, aunque formábamos parte de un pelotón de combate.
stops.quote_source: Teté Puebla, quoted in Bohemia, 'Gardenias guerrilleras'
suggested_refs: Bohemia, 'Gardenias guerrilleras,' on the outfitting of the Mariana Grajales Platoon

stops.name: Cerro Pelado: the Sherman and the three days
stops.date_confidence: Date attested: Friday 27 September 1958, a three-day action about four kilometres from the Estrada Palma mill, today Bartolomé Masó. The casualty figure was corrected by the verification pass: La Demajagua names five rebel bajas, casualties rather than deaths, among them lieutenants Raúl Verdecia and Luis Arturo Vázquez Matalobos and combatants Miguel López, René Ibarra and Juan Sardiñas Labrada, against 67 enemy dead and wounded. That no Mariana was hurt is Puebla's own claim; at least one account has the platoon's jefa wounded in the opening moments. Coordinate approximates the Estrada Palma area; the hill has no landmark-precise public figure.
stops.campa: The platoon's first collective action is a three-day stand under artillery and the guns of a Sherman tank, four kilometres from the sugar mill at Estrada Palma. The women hold their positions. Five rebels are hit, two of them lieutenants, and the other side counts sixty-seven dead and wounded across the three days. Puebla reports afterward that not one Mariana was touched. At least one account has the platoon's own jefa wounded in the opening minutes, and the two statements have never been reconciled.
stops.quote: Cuando me alcé no sabía ni cocinar, los horrores de la guerra me curtieron, al igual que las misiones encomendadas por el líder histórico de la Revolución.
stops.quote_source: Teté Puebla, interview in Trabajadores, 'Acompañar a Fidel en estos 50 años es lo mejor que puede haber pasado,' 8 January 2015
suggested_refs: La Demajagua's account of the Cerro Pelado combat, naming the five rebel casualties
sources: La Demajagua, on the Combate de Cerro Pelado, 27 September 1958

stops.name: Holguín: arrival on the night of the twentieth
stops.date_confidence: The arrival date of 20 October 1958 is given by Periódico 26's feature, fetched directly, and the four-woman composition of the detachment, with Isabel Rielo, Lilia Rielo and Edemis Tamayo, is attested there. Coordinate is Holguín city, an approximation for a detachment operating across the surrounding country.
stops.campa: Four of the thirteen are detached to the plains and sent north to reinforce Eddy Suñol's command toward Holguín: the two Rielo sisters, Edemis Tamayo, and Puebla. They come in at night and go straight into the province's operations, and inside a month she has been at the taking of Puerto Padre and at a crossroads called La Cadena, where until that day the people living there paid fifty cents to walk through. The mountains that hid the platoon for a year end here. Holguín is flat country and the army has trucks.
stops.quote: We arrived in Holguín on the night of the 20th and immediately joined the actions of the 26th of July Movement (M-26-7). I participated in the liberation of Puerto Padre; also in La Cadena, a place where residents had to pay 0.50 cents to pass through before that day.
stops.quote_source: Teté Puebla, quoted in 'Teté, a Woman Who Learned from Fidel,' Periódico 26, 2025, English-language edition
suggested_refs: Periódico 26, 'Teté, a Woman Who Learned from Fidel,' periodico26.cu

stops.name: The reservoir near Holguín: eleven rifles at dawn
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The dawn action against two trucks and a jeep near a reservoir, with two rebels wounded and eleven rifles captured, and the Radio Rebelde broadcast that followed, come from Periódico 26's account and from Puebla's own memoir; the reservoir is unnamed in every source reached, so the coordinate falls back on Holguín city. Suñol's letter singling her out is memoir-only.
stops.campa: At first light the detachment takes two trucks and a jeep on the road beside a reservoir that no source names. Two rebels are wounded. Eleven rifles change hands, which in this war is the actual currency, since a rifle taken is one the other side is no longer carrying. Radio Rebelde broadcasts the action within days, which is how a province learns that the women who spent a year in the sierra are down on the plain. Suñol writes a letter singling her out by name. The letter has not been found.
suggested_refs: Radio Rebelde bulletins, late October 1958, on the Holguín road actions
sources: Periódico 26, 'Teté, a Woman Who Learned from Fidel'
Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003

stops.name: Los Güiros: command falls to the girl from Yara
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, downgraded by the verification pass. That commander Eddy Suñol was wounded at Los Güiros, was evacuated, and that the Marianas took over is corroborated in outline by Cuban press and by Granma's Rielo retrospective. But no source either pass reached dates the combat to 2 November 1958, and none locates the hamlet, so the coordinate is a rough midpoint between Holguín and Velasco given here at false precision and flagged as such. The mutual-death pact Puebla describes with Rielo at this moment is her testimony alone.
stops.campa: The operation is meant to wreck Batista's scheduled elections. Suñol is hit early and carried off the field by Rielo's party, and the ranking fighter left standing is a seventeen-year-old who has never commanded anything larger than herself. It is the one occasion in her war where the record, thin as it is, shows her giving orders rather than carrying them, and that same record cannot say what day it was or where the hamlet stood. She commands. The detachment takes most of the opposing group and its weapons.
suggested_refs: Cuban press accounts of the Los Güiros combat and Eddy Suñol's wounding
sources: EcuRed, Escambray and Trabajadores accounts of Los Güiros
Granma, 'Dos 9 de abril, una misma visión revolucionaria,' 9 April 2014
Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003

stops.name: Bayamo: the first of January
stops.date_confidence: That she was in Bayamo when Batista fled is attested by English Wikipedia and Periódico 26, cross-checked, though her personal location that day rests ultimately on her own account. That she ended the war a first lieutenant, alongside Isabel Rielo and five other platoon members, is a reconstruction from her oral history and official biographical material, with no promotion order reached.
stops.campa: Batista leaves the country before dawn and the news reaches Bayamo, where Puebla is. She is eighteen years old and a first lieutenant, a rank she shares with Isabel Rielo and with five others of the thirteen. Two years and four months earlier she was enrolled at a teachers' college in Manzanillo with the intention of teaching primary school. She has not been back to Yara since the summer of 1957. Castro sends word for the Marianas to come to Santiago and ride in the column going west.
suggested_refs: Rebel Army rank rolls for the Mariana Grajales Platoon, December 1958
sources: Periódico 26, 'Teté, a Woman Who Learned from Fidel'

segments.name: The Caravan and the War Victims

stops.name: Santiago de Cuba: the Caravan of Liberty sets out
stops.date_confidence: Attested. A photograph in Wikimedia Commons, captioned 'Teté Puebla, segunda jefa del pelotón Mariana Grajales, durante el avance de la Caravana, enero de 1959,' places her in the convoy as deputy commander. Coordinate is the corpus's canonical Santiago de Cuba pin; the exact departure point in the city was not verified.
stops.campa: The column that leaves Santiago for Havana takes a week to cross the island because it stops in every town along the road, and the Marianas ride in it. A photographer catches Puebla in the advance and captions her by her function rather than by her name alone: second in command of the Mariana Grajales Platoon. The caption, and not any roster or order, is what fixes her rank in the record of the Caravan. She is eighteen and has been at war for two years.
suggested_refs: Wikimedia Commons, 'Teté Puebla segunda jefa del pelotón Mariana Grajales durante el avance de la Caravana, enero de 1959'
sources: fidel_castro.journey.json, chapter 'The Caravan of Liberty', stop 'Santiago de Cuba: the revolution begins now'

stops.name: Havana: the caravan arrives
stops.date_confidence: The Caravan's arrival in Havana on 8 January 1959 is attested; Puebla's presence in the convoy is attested by the Commons photograph record. The exact route and endpoint inside the city were not pinned down by either pass, so the coordinate is the corpus's canonical Havana pin.
stops.campa: The convoy comes into Havana on the eighth of January. It is the first time she has seen the capital, and by every account reached the first time she has been outside Oriente province. Within the year she will be posted back to Oriente, and it will be a decade before she lives in this city, but the Havana she enters this week on a truck at eighteen is the one that will still be sending her to parliament at eighty-five. The Marianas are not disbanded. They are never given anything further to do as a platoon.
suggested_refs: Press photography of the Caravan of Liberty entering Havana, 8 January 1959

stops.name: Santiago de Cuba: the Department of Assistance to War Victims
stops.date_confidence: The appointment is attested by English Wikipedia, which gives January 1959 and seats the Department for Care of War Victims in Santiago de Cuba. Two research lenses proposed conflicting exact dates, 8 January and 4 February 1959, and neither is supported: 8 January is the day the Caravan reached Havana, where the same file places her. The day given here is an ordering device inside the attested month. Promotion to captain on 24 May 1959 is a reconstruction from official profiles, with no order reached. The individual payment claims in her memoir, including to the family of Eutimio Guerra, are uncorroborated.
stops.campa: Castro puts her in charge of assistance to the victims of the war and their families in Oriente: burned houses rebuilt, pensions arranged, orphans schooled. The same is done for the dependents of men who fought on the other side. She is eighteen when she takes it, and in May she is made captain. No ledger from the department survives anywhere reachable, and the individual payments she describes rest on her word. The rule she quotes for the work is that before pain the homeland makes no distinction.
stops.quote: Celia es la mujer más grande que he conocido.
stops.quote_source: Teté Puebla, interview in Trabajadores, 'Acompañar a Fidel en estos 50 años es lo mejor que puede haber pasado,' 8 January 2015
suggested_refs: Records of the Departamento de Asistencia a las Víctimas de Guerra y sus Familiares, Oriente, 1959-1963
sources: Teté Puebla, Marianas en combate, Pathfinder Press, 2003

stops.name: Havana: married to Raúl Castro Mercader
stops.date_confidence: Attested by English Wikipedia, which names the husband and the three children Fidel, Raúl and Laura. He is no relation to Raúl Castro Ruz. The year 1960 is given without a month or a day, so the date defaults to the first of January, and the city is inferred rather than documented.
stops.campa: She marries Raúl Castro Mercader, a Rebel Army officer of no relation to the Castro brothers, who will end his career a brigadier general of the Revolutionary Armed Forces and serve in Angola. Where in 1960 the wedding happened, and on what day, no source reached says; a single encyclopaedia entry gives the bare year and nothing else. They have three children and name them Fidel, Raúl and Laura. The marriage lasts fifty-four years and ends with his death in 2014.
suggested_refs: Granma obituary of Raúl Castro Mercader, 3 September 2014, for his service record

stops.name: Habana Libre: the Federation of Cuban Women
stops.date_confidence: Corrected sourcing. The FMC founding date of 23 August 1960 is attested. Her leadership role in the organisation is attested; founding membership is not. Coordinate is the corpus's Habana Libre pin, used for the FMC founding elsewhere; the actual hall is not named in any source reached.
stops.campa: The island's separate women's organisations are merged into one Federation under Vilma Espín, and Puebla comes to sit on its national leadership. She is nineteen, a captain, and a veteran of a platoon that had to be argued into existence rifle by rifle. Whether she was in the room on the founding day is a question the sources do not answer: the profile that was read as naming her a founder names her instead to the Dirección Nacional, which is a different thing.

stops.name: Havana: the families of Playa Girón
stops.date_confidence: Attested that her war-victim assistance department served the families affected by the Bay of Pigs invasion of April 1961 and that she reported being mobilised, though not in a field-combat command role. Her personal location during the three days is not documented; the coordinate is the corpus's canonical Havana pin and stands for the administration rather than for her presence at the landing.
stops.campa: An invasion force lands at the Bay of Pigs and is finished in seventy-two hours, and the department she runs inherits the paperwork of it: the government dead counted, their families pensioned, their houses seen to, their children put on the schooling rolls. She is mobilised and is not sent to fight. The office she was handed in 1959 to clean up after one war is now counting the casualties of another. She will hold some version of it for the next sixty-five years.

stops.name: Santiago de Cuba: the education section of the Eastern Army
stops.date_confidence: Attested in official Cuban biographical profiles as synthesised by the research dossier, though neither pass refetched an institutional record for the posting. The Eastern Army's Santiago de Cuba base is the most defensible placement; the exact office is not confirmed. February 1963 is given without a day.
stops.campa: She is put over the education section of the Eastern Army's general staff, which means finding teachers and putting them in front of soldiers who cannot read. The Rebel Army recruited out of the same countryside she came from, and a great many of its men reached the war without a single year of schooling. She had one year of teachers' college in 1956 and did not finish it. The job now is to organise the schooling of an army, and she is twenty-two years old when it is handed to her.

stops.name: Havana: children's farms and the orphans of the war
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction from Puebla's oral history. The administration of children's farms and social-security services for war orphans within the Western Army in Havana is her own account; no institutional record was reached. Neither month nor day is given anywhere, so the date is purely an ordering device inside the reconstructed 1964-1966 window. Coordinate is the corpus's canonical Havana pin.
stops.campa: Transferred west, she administers children's farms and the social-security payments owed to the orphans of the war inside the Western Army. How many children, on how many farms, under what budget: her book says, and no other document reached says anything at all. The war has been over for five years. Its orphans are eight and nine years old now, and the state has decided to keep them on its own books rather than hand them back to relatives who cannot feed them.

stops.name: Havana: founding member of the Party
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the National Assembly's own profile, fetched directly, which calls her a founder of the Communist Party of Cuba and credits her with participation in all its congresses. The year 1965 is the constitution of the present party; the month and day are ordering devices. Her Central Committee service ran 1980 to 1986, a range rather than the single year the dossier first gave.
stops.campa: The party that has been called by three other names since 1959 is constituted as the Communist Party of Cuba, and she is on the founding roll. It is the credential that outranks the rifle in every decade that follows. Each posting she holds afterward, in agriculture, in the party's provincial machinery, in veterans' affairs, in the National Assembly, comes down through this list rather than through the Rebel Army rank she carried out of the sierra. The Assembly's profile credits her with every congress the party has held.

stops.name: Havana: the families of those sent abroad
stops.date_confidence: Attested in her oral history, Marianas en combate, as characterised in the dossier: General Staff chief Sergio del Valle placed her in a special FAR unit supporting the families of Cubans serving abroad and assisting disabled returnees. The missions named in her memoir are Algeria, Congo, Vietnam, Angola and Ethiopia. No source reached shows that she herself ever deployed abroad; this is a home-front administrative post and is staged at her own Havana pin accordingly.
stops.campa: Sergio del Valle puts her in a unit whose business is the households left behind when Cuba sends men out of the country: Algeria, the Congo, Vietnam, Angola, Ethiopia. Wages keep being paid, schools are arranged for the children, and the ones who come back without legs are found work. Puebla does not leave the island in this job, and no source reached shows her leaving it in any other one. Guevara had gone into the Congo the year before and told almost nobody where he was going.

stops.name: Jaruco: the Plan Ganadero Guaicanamar
stops.date_confidence: Attested in official biographical profiles and independently confirmed by EcuRed: Castro assigned her to direct the Plan Ganadero Guaicanamar at Jaruco from March 1969 to October 1978. Coordinate corrected to the town of Jaruco, about 10 km north of the figure the research pool carried. Jaruco was in Havana province for the whole period and has been in Mayabeque province only since the 2011 split. Production figures, budgets and the executions she reports in the area rest on her memoir alone.
stops.campa: Castro assigns her personally to run a cattle development scheme around Jaruco, and she works nine and a half years at it: fields, herds, and men who have not previously taken instruction from a woman on the subject of livestock. She recruits women into paid agricultural work and reports opening more than twelve schools in the district. The production figures, the budgets and the executions she says took place there all come out of her own book. Nobody has published a set of numbers from the other direction.

stops.name: Havana: the military section of the Party in the province
stops.date_confidence: Attested in official biographical profiles as synthesised in the dossier; no independent institutional roster was reached by either pass. Central Committee membership ran from 1980 to 1986 and is corroborated in the English-language biographical record. The coordinate is the corpus's canonical Havana pin; the party's provincial headquarters address is not confirmed.
stops.campa: She comes off the cattle plan in October 1978 and into the party's provincial apparatus in Havana, heading its military section. What she actually did in the post is described in no document reached. Celia Sánchez, the one person Puebla had ever publicly named as her model for how the work was to be done, dies in January of 1980. In the same year Puebla is elected to the Central Committee, where she sits for six years. The provincial posting runs until 1985.

stops.name: Havana: the combatants and the martyrs' families
stops.date_confidence: Attested. English Wikipedia independently corroborates her 1985 appointment as director of the Department for Care of Veterans and Martyrs. Neither month nor day is given, so the date defaults to the first of January. Her role in Operación Tributo, the 1989-1990 repatriation of Cuban dead from Africa, is noted in the dossier without a defined operational function. Isabel Rielo's death on 9 April 1989 is attested by Granma's 2014 retrospective.
stops.campa: From 1985 she directs services for combatants, for the families of Cubans serving abroad, and for the families of the dead the state calls martyrs. It is the same department she was handed at eighteen in Santiago de Cuba, grown to national size and to a second war's worth of casualties. When Cuba brings its Angola dead home in 1989 and 1990 under the name Operación Tributo, the caskets arrive into a system she has been running for four years. Isabel Rielo, who outshot her at La Plata and led the platoon for the rest of the war, dies on the ninth of April 1989.

stops.name: Havana: the first Cuban woman to be made general
stops.date_confidence: Attested by English Wikipedia, EcuRed and La Demajagua, cross-checked: promoted brigadier general on 24 July 1996, the first Cuban woman of general officer rank, in a ceremony that also advanced her husband Raúl Castro Mercader and Luis Alfonso Zayas. Her 1994 promotion to colonel is likewise attested. EcuRed quotes the promotion order's phrase about the dedication of her exemplary life. The ceremony venue is not specified in any source reached; the coordinate is an approximate central Havana government placement.
stops.campa: Made colonel in 1994 and brigadier general two years after that, the first woman in the country to hold general officer rank. The order Castro signs cites the dedication of her exemplary life to the worthy cause of the people, and the same ceremony advances her husband and Luis Alfonso Zayas. She is fifty-five. She has not commanded troops in the field since a hamlet called Los Güiros in November 1958, and she spends the following thirty years telling interviewers she would rather not be announced by the rank.
stops.quote: Toda mi vida la he dedicado a la Revolución. Si volviera a nacer haría lo mismo. Es un compromiso y un extraordinario honor ser la primera cubana que ostenta tan alto grado militar. No defraudaré a mi pueblo.
stops.quote_source: Teté Puebla on her promotion to brigadier general, 24 July 1996, in Cubainformación, 'Teté Puebla: La Generala, en persona,' interview by Luis Báez
suggested_refs: The promotion order of 24 July 1996, signed by Fidel Castro

stops.name: Havana: the bones brought back from Vallegrande
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and a placement made deliberately conservative. Official profiles credit her with participation in the 1997 reception of the remains identified as Guevara and his companions, without defining a role, and neither research pass could establish whether she was at the Santa Clara interment or at an earlier Havana reception. Rather than stage her at a ceremony she may not have attended, the stop sits at her own Havana pin and the Santa Clara question is left open.
stops.campa: Bones dug out of a pit beside a Bolivian airstrip come home thirty years after they were put there in secret, and Puebla, whose department handles the dead of the Revolution, is credited with a part in receiving them. Which part, and in which city, no source consulted will say, and whether she went to Santa Clara is not recorded anywhere. The last time she saw Guevara he was choosing her, out of a column of armed men, to walk into an enemy camp with a white flag and no weapon. She was seventeen then.
suggested_refs: Cuban state records of the October 1997 reception and interment of the remains identified as Ernesto Guevara

stops.name: Santiago de Cuba: Hero of the Republic of Cuba
stops.date_confidence: The date is attested across EcuRed, Wikipedia and search-corroborated sources: the title Hero of the Republic of Cuba, with the Order of Playa Girón, conferred by Fidel Castro on 2 December 2001. Two corrections apply. The occasion was the 45th anniversary of the Granma landing and FAR Day, not the 40th anniversary of the FAR as first written. And no source reached places the decoration ceremony in Havana; Granma's edition of 2 December 2001 reports the national military review for the 45th anniversary at the Plaza Antonio Maceo in Santiago de Cuba, where Castro spoke, which is why the coordinate is Santiago. Her presence in either city on the day remains undocumented and this placement is a judgement call.
stops.campa: On the forty-fifth anniversary of the Granma landing, marked that year with a military review at the Plaza Antonio Maceo, Castro confers on her the title Hero of the Republic of Cuba together with the Order of Playa Girón. It is the highest honour the state has to give. She has been in its service for forty-five years, counted from the schoolgirl selling bonds on the Manzanillo road. Where she stood while it was conferred, in Santiago or in Havana, is in no source either research pass reached.
suggested_refs: Granma, 2 December 2001, on the 45th anniversary review at the Plaza Antonio Maceo, Santiago de Cuba

stops.name: Havana: the interviews that became Marianas en combate
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The interviews underlying the book were conducted with her in Havana on 18 November 2000 and 1 March 2002. Pathfinder Press published the Spanish edition as Marianas en combate, 119 pages, ISBN 978-0-87348-963-8, and the English as Marianas in Combat, 115 pages, ISBN 978-0-87348-957-7, with an introduction by Mary-Alice Waters and a foreword by Juan Almeida Bosque; a Farsi edition followed, ISBN 964-7703-19-8. The publication happened in New York and is cited here rather than staged as her own stop, since she did not travel to it.
stops.campa: An editor from a New York publishing house sits with her in Havana across two sessions sixteen months apart and takes down the war. Nearly everything the world knows from the inside about the Mariana Grajales Platoon comes out of those two afternoons: the caltrops at Yara, the fever at El Hombrito, the mule, the armband, the coin at fifty metres. It is a woman of sixty remembering being seventeen. Pathfinder prints it in Spanish and in English in 2003, and afterward in Farsi.
suggested_refs: Teté Puebla, Marianas in Combat, Pathfinder Press, New York, 2003, introduction by Mary-Alice Waters, foreword by Juan Almeida Bosque

stops.name: Colón Cemetery: the FAR pantheon
stops.date_confidence: Attested directly by Granma's obituary of 3 September 2014, which records the death of reserve brigadier general Raúl Castro Mercader, names the Revolutionary Armed Forces pantheon at the Necrópolis Cristóbal Colón as the site of the funeral honours, and captions a photograph identifying 'la general de brigada Tete Puebla y demás familiares' among the mourners. stops.campa: Her husband dies in Havana and is buried with military honours in the pantheon of the Revolutionary Armed Forces at the Colón cemetery. Granma runs the obituary with a photograph of the honours, and the caption names her by rank before it names her as the widow: the brigadier general Tete Puebla and other family members. They had been married fifty-four years. They had been promoted to general on the same afternoon in July 1996, standing in the same line of officers.

stops.name: Havana: fifty years in civilian clothes
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Coordinate is the corpus's canonical Havana pin.
stops.campa: A trade-union paper interviews her on the anniversary of the Caravan's arrival in Havana, and she explains why she is almost never photographed in uniform. She is seventy-four. Of Celia Sánchez she says what she has been saying for fifty years. She talks about her three children, about the mountain, about not having known how to cook when she went up it, and about the defence budget, which she says she cannot understand anyone questioning while the largest power on earth is pointed at the island.

stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Mesa Redonda programme page at mesaredonda.cubadebate.cu for 6 March 2015, cited in the dossier as programme metadata and not refetched by the second pass. The studio location is approximated to central Havana; the exact ICRT address is not confirmed. The quotation is taken from the Trabajadores interview of two months earlier and is attributed there.

The title is Teté Puebla, la Generala, en persona. She tells the war again, to an audience born decades after it ended, and the title does the work the state wants done: one word, feminine, singular, definite. There has only ever been one. stops.name: Havana: Fidel and the advancement of Cuban women
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Interview published in Granma International on 19 August 2016 under the title 'Fidel and the advancement of Cuban women.' The quotation is given in English as published and is her recollection of something Castro taught the Marianas; the original Spanish wording was not checked by either pass. Castro dies three months later.
stops.campa: Three months before Castro's death, Granma International prints her on the subject of what he did for Cuban women, and she answers it by quoting back to the interviewer the thing he told the thirteen of them in the sierra while the men in the column were still objecting to the rifles. She is seventy-five, and she has been repeating that sentence in public since 1959. The Cuban state has printed it under photographs of the Mariana Grajales Platoon for two generations.
stops.quote: a people where men and women fight together, is an invincible people
stops.quote_source: Teté Puebla, recalling Fidel Castro, in Granma International, 'Fidel and the advancement of Cuban women,' 19 August 2016

stops.name: The Capitolio: sworn in as a deputy
stops.date_confidence: Corrected. The National Assembly profile's phrase 'desde su Primera Legislatura' means since her first legislature, not since the Assembly's first legislature of 1976, and the research pass's reading of it as the latter collapsed on inspection. EcuRed gives her ratification for the IX Legislature on 18 April 2018; Wikipedia gives 2017. The venue is also corrected: ordinary Assembly sessions have met at the restored Capitolio Nacional since 2018, not at the Palacio de Convenciones.
stops.campa: She enters the National Assembly at seventy-seven, in the legislature that replaces Raúl Castro as head of state, and is seated on the National Defence Commission. The chamber is the old Capitolio, raised under Machado in 1929 in imitation of the one in Washington, abandoned by the Revolution for half a century and reopened for the parliament in the same year she arrives in it. Two sources give two different years for her arrival, 2017 and 2018, and the point has not been settled.
stops.quote: He tenido el privilegio y la suerte de estar al lado de Fidel, primero en la Sierra Maestra y en todo este tiempo de Revolución, que para mí es lo más grande junto a mis tres hijos, formados en bien de esta sociedad.

stops.name: San Miguel del Padrón: the Tenth Legislature
stops.date_confidence: The municipality is confirmed directly by the Assembly's own profile: deputy for San Miguel del Padrón, Havana, in the Tenth Legislature, 2023 to 2028, and a member of the National Defence Commission. She sits again on the National Defence Commission, which for a reserve brigadier general of eighty-two is the obvious committee to be put on. Her international work in the Assembly runs to friendship groups with Laos, Cambodia and Mongolia. The legislature runs to 2028, by which time she will be eighty-seven.
stops.quote: No entiendo cómo alguien puede cuestionar que hablemos de defensa, si estamos amenazados por la mayor potencia mundial.
stops.quote_source: Teté Puebla, interview in Trabajadores, 8 January 2015

stops.date_confidence: Attested and upgraded by the verification pass. stops.name: Havana: eighty-five
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. A public congratulation from the Revolutionary Armed Forces on her eighty-fifth birthday is referenced by ACN under the headline 'Felicitan Fuerzas Armadas a Tete Puebla en su 85 cumpleanos,' found by search but not fetched in full by either pass. Her continuing status as a sitting deputy, reserve brigadier general and ACRC vice president is attested by the Assembly's current profile. She is still a deputy, still on the defence commission, still vice president of the veterans' association, and still, as far as anything reachable can establish, alive and at work in Havana. The Assembly's profile page lists her among its sitting members and gives no other news. Sixty-nine years earlier a fifteen-year-old in Manzanillo was selling bonds for a movement that had so far been beaten in every engagement it fought.
